title: Festive Season Ethnic Wear: What to Stock and When to Order
description: Plan your festive and wedding season ethnic wear stock: which styles to carry, how early to order, and how to avoid leftover stock after the season.

sections.heading: Plan backwards from your busiest weeks
body: Festive and wedding seasons bring the year's biggest spike in ethnic wear sales, but the stock has to be on your shelves before customers start shopping. Mark your busiest weeks on a calendar, such as the main festivals in your region and the local wedding dates, then plan to have stock in hand a few weeks earlier.
Order in two waves. The first wave arrives early and tests what your customers respond to this year. The second wave, placed once you see what is selling, tops up the winners before the peak.

sections.heading: Build a range that covers every budget
body: Festive shoppers range from someone buying a single kurti for a puja to a family buying outfits for a whole wedding. A good range has something at each level: everyday printed kurtis and kurta sets at the entry price, embroidered anarkalis and festive sets in the middle, and lehengas, sarees and sherwanis for special occasions.
On GarmentBazaar you can filter the Ethnic & Occasion department by budget per piece, which makes it easier to fill each price level without losing track of your spend.
bullets: Entry: printed kurtis, cotton kurta sets, dupattas
Middle: anarkalis, festive co-ord sets, men's kurta sets

sections.heading: Do not forget men and kids
body: Families often shop together for festivals and weddings. Stocking men's kurta sets, Indo-western jackets and kids' ethnic sets alongside your women's range turns one sale into three and gives customers a reason to finish their shopping with you.
Kids' ethnic wear is often bought at the last minute, so keep a sensible range of sizes in stock right up to the festival.

sections.heading: Colours and fabrics that move in festive months
body: Bright, celebratory colours such as reds, maroons, yellows, greens and pinks tend to lead in festive weeks, while pastels and ivory are popular for daytime functions. Mix both so customers can find something for every event.

Think about comfort too. Lighter fabrics suit warmer regions and long functions, while heavier embroidery and richer fabrics suit evening events and cooler months. Your own sales from last season are the best guide to what works in your town.

sections.heading: Order small first, then reorder what sells
body: Festive stock is a big investment, so the risk of leftover pieces is real. Start each new style at the brand's MOQ, watch which ones sell in the first weeks, and reorder those at two or three times the MOQ before the peak.
Use the margin calculator before you commit to premium pieces. A lehenga that ties up a lot of money needs a margin that justifies the shelf space and the risk.

sections.heading: Display and sell festive stock well
body: How you show festive stock matters as much as what you buy. Put your most colourful and occasion-ready pieces near the entrance and in your window, and group complete looks together, such as a kurta set with a matching dupatta and juttis, so customers can picture the whole outfit.

Share new festive arrivals with your regular customers on WhatsApp a little before the rush, with the price and available sizes in each message. Many buyers in smaller towns decide where to shop based on what they see on their phone, and an early message brings them to your counter before they travel elsewhere.
bullets: Lead with occasion-ready colours at the entrance
Group complete looks, not single pieces
Share new arrivals on WhatsApp before the peak

sections.heading: Plan for after the season
body: Every season leaves some stock behind. Keep it small by stopping reorders of slower styles a couple of weeks before the peak, moving remaining festive pieces to the front of the shop afterwards, and bundling dupattas or accessories with kurtis to clear them without deep discounts.
Note which styles sold out and which stayed on the rack. That record is the most valuable input for next year's festive order.

faq.q: How early should I order festive ethnic wear?
faq.a: Aim to have your first wave of stock on the shelves a few weeks before your busiest festival or wedding dates, then place a second order for the styles that sell first.

faq.q: Which ethnic wear sells best for festivals?
faq.a: It varies by region and customer. Kurtis, kurta sets and festive co-ords usually sell in volume, while lehengas, sarees and sherwanis bring higher-value sales. Your last season's sales are the best guide.

faq.q: How do I avoid leftover festive stock?
faq.a: Start new styles at the MOQ, reorder only proven sellers, stop reorders shortly before the peak, and bundle slower pieces with accessories after the season.
